rationale: C13 is a highly plausible material drafting template. It uses the same statutory recital concerning the eight-hour limitation, invokes the same December 16, 1950 national emergency, identifies an urgent national objective requiring unusually rapid and efficient work, applies the extraordinary-emergency mechanism to public work performed by a named aeronautics agency, and closes with an indefinite presidential-termination clause. The child substantially adapts that framework from modernization of air-navigation facilities by the Civil Aeronautics Administration to the aeronautical and space program administered by NASA. C03 and C12 share the core statutory and emergency-law template, but their agency-specific predicates are shorter and less closely parallel the child's elaborated aeronautics rationale and duration clause.

shared_material.child_excerpt: WHEREAS by section 1 of the act of August 1, 1892, 27 Stat. 340, as amended by the act of March 3, 1913, 37 Stat. 726 (40 U.S.C. 321), the service or employment of all laborers and mechanics employed by the Government of the United States upon any public work of the United States is limited to eight hours in any one calendar day, except in case of extraordinary emergency
shared_material.parent_excerpt: WHEREAS by section 1 of the act of August 1, 1892, 27 Stat. 340, as amended by the act of March 3, 1913, 37 Stat. 726 (40 U.S.C. 321), the service or employment of all laborers and mechanics employed by the Government of the United States upon any public work of the United States is limited to eight hours in any one calendar day, except in case of extraordinary emergency
shared_material.explanation: The child reproduces the entire operative statutory recital essentially verbatim.

shared_material.child_excerpt: WHEREAS by [DIRECTIVE_REFERENCE] of December 16, 1950, the President proclaimed the existence of a national emergency and that emergency still exists
shared_material.parent_excerpt: WHEREAS by [DIRECTIVE_REFERENCE] of December 16, 1950, the President proclaimed the existence of a national emergency
shared_material.explanation: Both ground the suspension in the same proclaimed national emergency.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the attainment and maintenance by this Nation of a clearly leading role in aeronautical and space achievement has become a vital national objective; and WHEREAS in order to achieve this objective it is essential to conduct the Nation's aeronautical and space program ... with all possible speed and efficiency
shared_material.parent_excerpt: WHEREAS it is essential to the national defense that the Nation's system of air-navigation facilities be modernized in a very short period of time, and that such system be operated and maintained at the highest level of efficiency
shared_material.explanation: These recitals perform the same drafting function through closely parallel language: an aeronautics-related national objective must be pursued rapidly and at maximum efficiency.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the development and administration of our national aeronautical and space program are the primary responsibility of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration
shared_material.parent_excerpt: public work essential to the national defense being performed by the Civil Aeronautics Administration
shared_material.explanation: The child adapts the parent’s agency-specific application of the extraordinary-emergency machinery from the Civil Aeronautics Administration to NASA.

shared_material.child_excerpt: This order shall remain in force and effect during the period of the national emergency ... unless sooner terminated by Executive order of the President.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: This order shall continue in effect until terminated or revoked by the President.
shared_material.explanation: Both use a materially similar presidential-termination duration clause, with the child additionally tying its outside limit to the national emergency.
